previous_paragraph: Interpreting Figure 4 reveals that both critical time delay indicators ( τcr,N and τcr,P) fail to accurately reflect the growing risk of instability arising from structural damage. Specifically, τcr,N exhibits misleading behavior as its normalized value increases with damage, falsely suggesting enhanced stability, while τcr,P remained nearly constant until exhibiting an abrupt drop, offering no advance warning. In contrast, the  GMP exhibits a more gradual decrease before the onset of instability, suggesting that the instability triggered by the degradation is closer to being caused by a gain amplification in the outer controller loop than a time delay, a mechanism that delay margins struggle to detect. To further illustrate this behavior, Figure 5 shows the corresponding open-loop gain and phase responses of Hymy1, highlighting how the outer-loop dynamics evolve with physical substructure degradation and can lead to instabilities.
actual_paragraph: Based on our observations in the laboratory, this instability is caused by the controller being initially tuned to both overcome the specimen's relatively high stiffness and also achieve the required tracking performance. As the specimen degrades and loses stiffness, it becomes easier to move, so the same corrective control action is likely to overshoot more and produce a larger displacement response than under the original stiffness condition. The extent of this response amplification is influenced by the specimen mass, and the resulting interaction between the degraded specimen and the transfer system, which includes this controller, can eventually drive the system toward instability. It's important to note that, despite being observed experimentally, these behaviors are not universal, as the dominant instability mechanism and the performance of each indicator can change substantially depending on the specific dynamics of the transfer system and the physical substructure.
next_paragraph: This study aims to present an online stability indicator for quantifying the system's robustness against different instability mechanisms driven by unmodeled dynamics or unforeseen disruptions, while also aiming to provide a sufficient time frame for effective intervention before instability occurs. To address a notable gap in the literature, this study focuses on the transfer system's internal stability, giving special consideration to physical system degradation, as it can manifest during an experiment in various forms, including, but not limited to, excessive specimen damage, the activation of unintended structural failure mechanisms, or the mechanical failure of test set-up components such as fasteners. Additionally, a controller switching strategy is proposed to leverage the stability indicator for real-time corrective action when degradation threatens system stability.
